html:
This bar covers the kingdom of Siam, renamed Thailand in 1939, under the Chakri dynasty, which has ruled from Bangkok since 1782. It is the only country in Southeast Asia never colonised by a European power.

After a Burmese army destroyed Ayutthaya in 1767, the general Taksin drove the Burmese out and ruled from Thonburi. In 1782 he was overthrown, and his general Chao Phraya Chakri became king as Rama I. He moved the capital across the river to Bangkok and rebuilt the kingdom on Ayutthaya's model.

In the 19th century Britain and France closed in from both sides. Siam survived by bending:

  • Mongkut (Rama IV) signed the Bowring Treaty with Britain in 1855, opening Siam to free trade on unequal terms.
  • Chulalongkorn (Rama V, 1868 to 1910) abolished slavery, built railways, and remade the government on European lines.
  • Siam gave up claims to Laos and western Cambodia to France, and its Malay states to Britain, to keep its core.

In 1932 a group of officials and officers ended absolute monarchy in the Siamese revolution. Military governments dominated what followed. Thailand allied with Japan in the Second World War and with the United States in the Cold War, serving as a base during the Vietnam War. Since then it has grown into a middle-income economy and a centre of tourism, while coups and street protests have repeatedly interrupted elections. The king remains a revered and legally protected figure.
